argument: Building on the idea that we are our circumstances, Ortega argues that late-19th-century classical liberalism inflated equality from a value to be prioritized into a value to be fetishized, granting mediocre opinions unprecedented cultural authority and producing the 'mass man'—a psychological type, found in any social class, who is entirely self-satisfied and treats their own ideas as valid simply because those ideas exist in their head. Ortega calls this a spiritual barbarism structurally similar to fascism, since both refuse to justify their views against any outside standard, and warns that mass entitlement erodes the very historical achievements and institutions it takes for granted. His remedy is not to restore a literal ruling class but to 'reinstate the aristocracy' as a personal, existentialist demand each person makes of themselves: pursue self-improvement and take seriously the history that constitutes both one's country and oneself.
keyIdeas: The 'mass man' is a psychological mentality, not an economic class; a billionaire can think with a mass mentality just as easily as anyone else.
Classical liberalism turned equality from a prioritized value into a fetishized one, giving mediocre opinions a legitimacy in public discourse they had never had before.
Ortega compares the mass man's inherited freedom to a dictator's or nepotistic boss's son: given power and freedom without earning the understanding and responsibility that should accompany it.
The mass mentality resembles fascism because both treat an idea as valid simply because it exists in one's own head, with no need to justify it against any external standard.

Reinstating the aristocracy does not mean restoring a ruling class; it is a personal, existentialist responsibility toward self-improvement and taking history seriously, since a person's identity, like a word's meaning, is built from a much longer history than their own lifetime.

terms.def: Ortega's term for a self-satisfied psychological type, present across all classes, who feels entitled to full participation in culture without earning or understanding it.
Ortega's term for a society where equality has been fetishized rather than prioritized, giving unqualified opinions undue weight.

For Ortega, the qualitative distinction between people who actively challenge their own prejudices and those who remain self-satisfied; 'reinstating' it is a personal responsibility, not a political program.
Ortega's description of the mass man as a new kind of barbarian: professionally learned yet culturally uncultured.
